passage: By the third night of her sister Jyoti's wedding in Bhilwara, Uma's feet were blistered and her smile felt glued on. One aunty had already said her lehenga was 'too simple for the bride's sister'. Another counted the sweets on the thali and sniffed. Uma had run between the caterer, the mehendi and Dadi's medicines since dawn. Then, during the pheras, she stood close enough to see Jyoti's hands shaking in Rakesh's, and heard Jyoti laugh nervously at the fourth round. Uma's eyes filled. Her big sister, who had shared her bed for twenty years, was stepping into a new life. The aunties could say what they liked. Uma stopped watching them and watched Jyoti.

qa.q: Where was Jyoti's wedding?
qa.a: In Bhilwara.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling during the pheras?
qa.a: Uma felt moved and a little sad, eyes filling as she saw her sister step into a new life, forgetting the aunties' comments.

qa.q: What helped Uma get through the exhausting wedding?
qa.a: Shifting her attention from the relatives' judgements to the real meaning of the ceremony, her sister's new stage of life.

qa.q: How might Jyoti have felt during the pheras?
qa.a: Jyoti seemed nervous and emotional, her hands shaking and her laugh uneasy as she began a new life.

grounding: Shows a young adult at a big family wedding who feels joy, pressure and exhaustion under relatives' judgements, and finds the real meaning in the new stage it marks.

passage: At her cousin Marek's wedding in a village outside Gdańsk, Astrid, twenty-two, had been on her feet for fourteen hours. The Polish side of the family had opinions about everything: her short hair, her Swedish dress 'like a nightgown', whether the pierogi were as good as at the last wedding. She had danced every polka she was dragged into and smiled till her cheeks ached. Around midnight she slipped outside with a glass of water. Through the window she saw Marek's grandmother pin a lace veil on the bride for the unveiling ritual, both of them crying. Astrid leaned on the wall and let it land: Marek, who once taught her to ride a bike, was married. The rest was noise.

qa.q: How long had Astrid been on her feet?
qa.a: Fourteen hours.

qa.q: What was Astrid feeling as she leaned on the wall outside?
qa.a: She felt tired but tender and moved, finally taking in that Marek, who taught her to ride a bike, was married.

qa.q: What helped Astrid separate the wedding's meaning from the show?
qa.a: Stepping outside for a quiet moment and watching the veil ritual, which reminded her of the real change in Marek's life.

qa.q: How might Marek's grandmother have felt pinning the veil?
qa.a: She seemed deeply moved, crying with the bride as she marked the start of a new stage.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult at a big wedding who feels joy, pressure and tiredness as relatives judge dress and food, and who finds the real meaning in the new stage the ceremony marks.

passage:
Hey Sumit,

Sorry I didn't reply all week. Didi's wedding ate me alive.

The good parts first: Didi's face at the jaimala, and Papa dancing to a song from 1994 as if nobody was watching. I cried twice. Don't tell anyone.

The rest: five days of relatives inspecting everything. Tauji said the paneer was rubbery. The groom's aunt asked why the pheras started twelve minutes late. Someone's Bua told me my sherwani was too plain for the bride's brother. I was in charge of the band, three cars and forty room keys, and I slept four hours a night.

On the last night I found Didi alone on the terrace in her lehenga, eating cold puri. She said, "Forget the paneer. I got married today." That fixed it for me. The rest was a show. That part was real.

Back Monday. You're buying chai.

Akash

qa.q: How many hours a night did Akash sleep?
qa.a: Akash slept four hours a night.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Akash have through the wedding week?
qa.a: Akash felt joy at Didi's jaimala and Papa's dancing, pressure from relatives' judgements, and deep tiredness from the jobs and little sleep.

qa.q: What helped Akash separate meaning from show?
qa.a: Didi's words on the terrace, 'I got married today', reminded him that the marriage was the real point, not the relatives' verdicts.

qa.q: How did Didi seem to see the wedding by the last night?
qa.a: Didi seemed calm and content, brushing off the paneer complaints because what mattered had happened.

grounding: Shows a young adult at a big family wedding feeling joy, pressure and exhaustion, and separating the real meaning from the show.

passage:
You asked about my nikah. I'm Afreen, and honestly I remember it in two layers.

Layer one: relatives. My Phuppo checking the embroidery on my gharara and calling it simple. Two aunties arguing about whether the biryani had enough saffron. Someone asking my mother, loudly, how much the hall cost. My feet hurt, my face hurt from smiling, and at one point I hid in the washroom for ten minutes just to breathe.

Layer two: the moment the qazi sahab asked me, "Qubool hai?" and I looked at Abbu's face. He was crying and trying not to. I said yes three times, and it felt as if the ground under me had shifted.

My friend Trisha told me afterwards, "You looked like you were somewhere else." I was. I was in layer two.

Nobody will remember the saffron. I'll remember that.

qa.q: How long did Afreen hide in the washroom?
qa.a: Afreen hid in the washroom for ten minutes just to breathe.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling during the relatives' comments?
qa.a: Afreen felt pressured and exhausted, feet and face aching from smiling, needing to hide just to breathe.

qa.q: What helped Afreen hold on to the meaning of the day?
qa.a: Focusing on the moment of saying yes and on Abbu's face, the real marker of a new stage, instead of the relatives' assessments.

qa.q: What might the moment have been like for Afreen's Abbu?
qa.a: Abbu was deeply moved, crying and trying not to, as his daughter said yes.

grounding: Shows a young adult at her own wedding feeling pressure and exhaustion from relatives' judgements while holding on to the ceremony's real meaning.

passage:
Five days before: At Vandana didi's mehendi, Mami looked Sharmila up and down. "That colour? For the bride's cousin? People will talk." Sharmila, twenty-one, laughed it off and changed anyway.

Wedding day: She was up at four, ran between the caterers and the pandit, fixed the bride's dupatta pins, and argued with the band about the order of songs. By the pheras her feet were blistered in her new sandals. When Vandana didi and Jiju took the seventh step, Sharmila cried so hard her kajal ran, and didn't care who saw.

Two days after: At breakfast, Mami started on the caterers' dal. Sharmila put down her cup. "Mami, didi is married and happy. That's what the whole thing was for." Mami blinked. Then, surprisingly, she nodded.

qa.q: When was Sharmila up on the wedding day?
qa.a: She was up at four.

qa.q: What did Sharmila feel as the seventh step was taken?
qa.a: Sharmila felt overwhelming joy, crying hard enough to ruin her kajal and not caring who saw.

qa.q: How did Sharmila answer Mami's criticism at breakfast, and why did it work?
qa.a: She calmly reminded Mami that the bride was married and happy, the real point, which moved the talk from show to meaning.

qa.q: How might Mami have felt when Sharmila spoke up?
qa.a: Mami was surprised, then seemed to accept it, perhaps seeing she had been focused on the show.

grounding: Shows a young adult at a family wedding moving through joy, pressure and exhaustion, and naming the ceremony's real meaning over the show.

passage:
Shankar, you're dreading your sister's wedding? Let your Himani athai tell you about mine. I was twenty-two. Four days of functions in Coimbatore. On the first night, relatives inspected my saree border, counted the gold, and said the payasam had too little cashew. My feet bled in new sandals. I smiled until my cheeks ached. By the reception I was so tired I cried in the toilet between photographs.
Then, on the last morning, before the muhurtham, my Appa came into the room. He held my hands and just said, "New life, kanna." Suddenly all the noise went quiet. I remembered what the day was really for: not the cashews or the photos, but me and your uncle starting something together. I walked out calmer. So during your sister's wedding, when the aunties talk, find one quiet minute with her. Remember what it's for.

qa.q: How old was Himani athai at her wedding?
qa.a: Twenty-two.

qa.q: How did young Himani feel by the reception?
qa.a: She felt exhausted and overwhelmed, crying in the toilet between photographs.

qa.q: What was the turning point for young Himani, and why did it help?
qa.a: Her Appa holding her hands and saying "New life"; it reminded her the wedding marked a new stage, separating the real meaning from the show.

qa.q: How might her Appa have felt coming into the room that morning?
qa.a: He probably felt full of love and emotion, wanting a quiet moment with his daughter before she began her new life.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult at her wedding who feels joy, pressure and exhaustion, and finds meaning by seeing it as a new stage.
